West Africa · Nigeria · Diaspora

Pineapple, Pear & Tropical Hand Pies
8 Serves
30 min Active Time
22 min Bake Time

May 2026 Sunday Edition

Jump to Recipe
Region West Africa · Nigeria
Category Baking
Pillars Heritage · Science · Joy
Level Intermediate

My 12-year-old loves pie. Not the filling — the crust. He has always been that kid who eats around the fruit and saves the pastry for last, like it is the point. So I stopped making full pies and started making him hand pies instead. All crust. Maximum crunch. A jammy little pocket of tropical fruit inside that he tolerates because it is surrounded by the thing he actually came for.

These are pineapple and pear, spiced with ginger and cloves, sealed inside a dough built to shatter. The secret is frozen butter grated straight into cold flour — not cut in, not rubbed in, grated — so the fat stays in thin ribbons that puff and crunch in a hot oven the way a full pie crust can only dream of. It is faster than a whole pie, louder when you bite it, and Eni ate three before I could get the shot.

These fruits have been on West African tables for generations — not as novelty, not as borrowed flavors, but as pantry staples. Pineapple sold at the side of the road in Ibadan, peeled and quartered and dusted with salt. Pear sliced into salads, pressed into juices. I put them in pastry at 4am and dusted them with snow, and they tasted exactly like a Sunday should.

Heritage

The Fruit That
Was Always Ours

Pineapple and pear didn't arrive at our table. They were already there.

Before it was a pastry filling, it was breakfast in someone's compound in Lagos.

Pineapple has been cultivated across West and Central Africa since the 16th century, introduced through trade routes from South America and immediately absorbed into the fabric of daily life. By the time it reached colonial-era markets, it was already ours — sold by women at roadsides, pressed into drinks, sliced thick and handed to children as an afternoon snack. In Nigeria, pineapple is not an exotic ingredient. It is a staple. It is Tuesday.

African pear — the kind you find in Nigerian markets — is a different creature entirely from the European varieties that dominate American grocery shelves. Ube, as it is known in Igbo, has a buttery, avocado-rich flesh that softens in heat and carries a faint nuttiness that no canned pear can replicate. It is boiled in salted water and eaten alongside roasted corn. It is a food of community, of slowness, of sitting outside with people you love while something cooks.

When I built this filling, I wasn't reaching for West African flavor. I was reaching back to something that was already sitting there. Pineapple and pear together, spiced with ginger — the warming root that runs through so much of our cooking — and cloves, the spice that smells like harmattan and grandmothers and something you can't quite name. This is not fusion. This is just memory, in pastry form.

The best things you can put in a crust are the things that were already on your table before anyone told you they belonged there.

Full Batch · Wire Rack · Powdered Sugar · Morning Window Light

What this recipe does is give those flavors a new architecture. The hand pie is not a Nigerian form — but the filling inside it is unmistakably West African in its bones. Ginger that blooms in the heat of the oven. Pineapple that breaks down into a jammy sweetness with a bright, acidic edge. A lime finish that lifts the whole thing and makes you reach for the next one before you've finished the first.

Eni ate three. That is the highest possible review.

Science

Why I Grate the Butter
Instead of Cutting It In

Most pie dough recipes tell you to cut cold butter into flour using a pastry cutter or your fingers — working it until you have pea-sized pieces. It works. But pea-sized pieces are still thick enough to create pockets of fat that melt unevenly in the oven, sometimes leaving you with a crust that is flaky in one bite and doughy in the next.

Grating frozen butter changes the equation entirely. Frozen butter on a box grater produces thin, even ribbons that distribute through the flour in a way no cutter can replicate. Those ribbons stay cold longer, coat more surface area, and create a more consistent lamination through the dough. When the oven heat hits them, each ribbon produces its own pocket of steam — and it is that steam, multiplied hundreds of times across the surface of the pie, that makes the crust shatter rather than bend.

The Chemistry

Pastry flakiness is a function of fat distribution and water content. When butter melts in a hot oven, the water inside it — butter is roughly 15–18% water — turns to steam almost instantly. That steam pushes the layers of gluten-coated flour apart, creating the airy gaps we read as flake.

The key is keeping the fat cold until the oven does its work. Frozen butter grated fine stays colder longer than cut-in chunks because its surface area is greater and it warms more slowly. More cold fat going into the oven means more controlled, even steam release — and more consistent flake across the entire surface.

The tectonic fold amplifies this effect. Folding the dough in thirds, rotating, and repeating creates dozens of thin layers — each one separated by a film of butter. This is the same principle behind laminated doughs like croissants and rough puff pastry, applied to a standard hand pie dough with a fraction of the effort.

The result is a crust that shatters when you bite it — loud, dramatic, structural. Not doughy. Not soft. The kind of crust a 12-year-old eats three of before you can stop him.

The chilling window matters too. Two and a half hours minimum, not as an afterthought but as an active step. That rest allows the gluten to relax — making the dough easier to roll — and keeps the butter cold right up until it hits the oven. Skip it and you lose the crunch. Honor it and the crust does everything you want it to.

What you taste at the end is the payoff of temperature management. The outside shatters. The inside yields. The filling — jammy and bright and spiced — holds its shape because the cornstarch has thickened it into something stable, not wet. Every element is doing its job, and every bite sounds like Sunday morning.

Joy Through Precision

Why I Bake Before
the Boys Wake Up

It is 4am and the house is quiet in a way it will not be again for the rest of the day. The toddler will wake at 6 and the world will tilt immediately into need — cereal, Thomas the Tank Engine, the particular blanket, not that blanket, the other one. Eni will wake at 7 and need to be driven somewhere or talked through something or simply witnessed, which is its own kind of work. My foster daughter in Nigeria will text at some point and I will carry her situation with me all day the way I always do, like a second heartbeat.

But at 4am, none of that has started yet. At 4am it is just me and the flour and the frozen butter and the decision I made a long time ago that Sunday mornings belong to me.

I grated the butter into the flour before the coffee finished brewing. I folded the dough while the kitchen was dark except for the hood light over the stove. I chilled it, made the filling, chilled that too. By the time the sun came through the window at the angle that means it is actually morning and not just very early, the pies were in the oven and the whole house smelled like ginger and brown butter and something warm enough to stop you in the hallway.

Eni came downstairs and ate three before I got the shot. He didn't say anything about the pineapple or the pear or the spices. He said: "Mom, the crust is so good." And I thought: yes. Yes it is. That is exactly what I spent four hours building. I will take it.

This is why I bake before the world wakes up. Not because I need the silence, though I do. Not because the light is better for photographs, though it is. But because these four hours are the only ones in the week where the outcome of something is entirely within my control. The butter will behave if I keep it cold. The dough will rest if I give it time. The oven will do what I tell it. And at the end of it, there will be something real — something that shatters when you bite it and fills a plate and gets eaten by a boy who says the crust is so good and means it as the highest compliment he knows how to give.

Our Sunday Table — Recipe

Tropical Hand Pies

Pineapple & Pear · Ginger & Clove · Shattering Laminated Crust

8 Serves
30 min Active
22 min Bake
400°F Temperature

Ingredients

For the Dough

All-purpose flour
420g
Unsalted butter, frozen and grated
340g
Fine salt
1 tsp
Granulated sugar
1 tbsp
Ice water
120–180ml

For the Pineapple & Pear Filling

Canned pears, drained and diced small
425g (15oz)
Canned pineapple, drained and diced small
425g (15oz)
Brown sugar
3 tbsp
Unsalted butter
1 tbsp
Ground ginger
½ tsp
Ground cloves
¼ tsp
Fresh lime juice
1 tbsp
Cornstarch
1 tsp

To Finish

Egg, for egg wash
1 large
Powdered sugar, for dusting
to taste

Method

01

Grate the Butter

Freeze your butter for at least 30 minutes — it must be completely solid. Using a box grater, grate the frozen butter directly into your flour, salt, and sugar. Toss lightly with a fork between handfuls to coat the ribbons in flour and prevent clumping. Work quickly.

Do not use your hands to rub the butter in. The heat of your palms will melt it. Toss only.
02

Hydrate and Fold

Add ice water one tablespoon at a time, tossing with a fork after each addition, until the dough just comes together when pressed — shaggy, not smooth. Turn it out onto a lightly floured surface. Perform the tectonic fold: press the dough into a rough rectangle, fold it in thirds like a letter, rotate 90 degrees, fold again. Repeat twice more. The dough will look rough. That is correct.

Stop adding water the moment the dough holds together when pressed. Too much water develops gluten and toughens the crust.
03

Chill

Wrap the dough tightly in plastic wrap and refrigerate for a minimum of 2.5 hours. Do not rush this. The rest relaxes the gluten and keeps the butter cold.

04

Make the Filling

Dice pears and pineapple small — roughly 1cm pieces. Melt butter in a saucepan over medium heat. Add fruit, brown sugar, ginger, and cloves. Cook, stirring occasionally, until the liquid releases and then evaporates — about 8 minutes. Whisk cornstarch into lime juice and stir into the pan. Cook one more minute until thick and jammy. Transfer to a bowl and refrigerate until completely cold before filling.

Cold filling is non-negotiable. Warm filling will steam inside the pie and make the crust soggy from the inside.
05

Roll and Cut

Preheat oven to 400°F (200°C). Line a baking sheet with parchment. On a lightly floured surface, roll the dough to ⅛ inch thickness. Cut into rectangles approximately 4 × 5 inches — you will need pairs. Score or cut a small vent pattern into the tops before assembly.

06

Fill and Seal

Place a bottom rectangle on the baking sheet. Spoon 2–3 tablespoons of cold filling into the center, leaving a clear ½ inch border all around. Brush the border with egg wash. Press the top rectangle over firmly and crimp the edges with a fork to seal completely. Brush the top with egg wash.

Press and crimp firmly. Any unsealed edge will burst open in the oven and the filling will escape.
07

Bake

Bake at 400°F for 18–22 minutes until deep golden brown. The color you want is amber, not pale gold — that deep color is what tells you the crust has set and crunched through. Cool on the pan for 10 minutes before moving.

08

Dust and Serve

Sift powdered sugar generously over the cooled pies. Serve warm or at room temperature. Best eaten the day they are baked — the crust is loudest fresh from the oven.

The best thing you can bake for someone is the thing they didn't know they needed — a crust that shatters, a filling that holds, a Sunday morning that tastes like home even when home is a moving target.

May your Sundays be loud with the sound of something good.

— Temie Giwa-Tubosun · Our Sunday Table
